pages.title: About
pages.content:
Byte Notes is a small engineering notebook about backends, databases, tooling and the web platform. Every article starts as a problem met at work and ends as the write-up I wish I had found at the time.

What you will find here

Deep dives

Long, practical articles with code you can paste and adapt.

Field notes

Short lessons from incidents, migrations and code reviews.

Tools

The editor setups, scripts and habits that make the work smoother.

Have a topic you would like covered? Get in touch.

pages.title: Uses
pages.content:
The hardware, software and conventions behind these notes. Nothing here is sponsored; it is simply what works for me today.

Editor and terminal

  • A modal editor with a language server for every project
  • A tiling terminal with one tab per service
  • A monospaced font with clear zeros and ligatures turned off

Defaults for new projects

make dev      # start the app with live reload
make test     # unit tests, race detector on
make lint     # format, vet, static checks

Every repository gets the same three commands, so switching projects never means relearning the workflow.

posts.title: Graceful shutdowns in Go HTTP servers, step by step
posts.excerpt: Deploys should not drop requests. Here is the small amount of code that lets a Go server finish its work before it exits.
posts.content:
Every deploy sends your server a signal. What happens in the next few seconds decides whether a customer sees an error page or nothing at all. A graceful shutdown means three things: stop accepting new connections, let in-flight requests finish, and give up after a deadline.

The whole pattern

The standard library already does the hard part. http.Server.Shutdown closes the listeners, then waits for active connections to go idle. Your job is to call it at the right moment and to bound how long it may take.

ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
defer stop()

srv := &http.Server{Addr: ":8080", Handler: mux}
go func() {
    if err := srv.ListenAndServe(); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
        log.Fatalf("listen: %v", err)
    }
}()

<-ctx.Done() // wait for the signal
shutdownCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 15*time.Second)
defer cancel()
if err := srv.Shutdown(shutdownCtx); err != nil {
    log.Printf("forced shutdown: %v", err)
}

Things that still bite

  • Long-lived connections. WebSockets and streaming responses are hijacked, so Shutdown does not wait for them. Track them yourself.
  • Background goroutines. Workers started by handlers need their own context and a sync.WaitGroup.
  • The load balancer. Fail the readiness check first, wait a couple of seconds, then shut down, so no new traffic is routed to you.

Rule of thumb: the shutdown timeout should be shorter than the grace period your orchestrator gives the process, or it will be killed mid-drain.

Put this in a small helper once and every service you write gets zero-downtime deploys for free. It is one of the best returns on twenty lines of code you will find.

comments.author: Mira K.
comments.content: The readiness-check tip saved us. We were dropping a handful of requests on every rollout and never knew why.

comments.author: devon_r
comments.content: Worth adding: RegisterOnShutdown is handy for closing hijacked connections politely.

posts.title: Reading a PostgreSQL query plan without panic
posts.excerpt: EXPLAIN output looks intimidating until you know which three numbers to read first.
posts.content:
A slow query is a question, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE is the answer written in a slightly unfriendly dialect. Once you learn to read it from the inside out, it becomes the most useful tool in your database kit.

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT o.id, o.total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE c.region = 'north'
  AND o.created_at > now() - interval '30 days';

Start at the deepest node

Plans are trees. The most indented line runs first and feeds its parent. For each node, compare the estimated rows with the actual rows. A difference of ten times or more usually means stale statistics or a predicate the planner cannot see through.

The three numbers that matter

  1. actual time: the second value is when the node finished, in milliseconds.
  2. rows versus loops: multiply them to get the real row count.
  3. Buffers: shared hits are cheap, reads went to disk.

Most slow queries are not missing an index. They are missing an accurate estimate.

When estimates are wrong, run ANALYZE on the tables involved, consider extended statistics for correlated columns, and only then reach for a new index.

comments.author: Priya
comments.content: Multiplying rows by loops was the missing piece for me. Thank you!

posts.title: Container image layers, explained with one tiny service
posts.excerpt: Why your image rebuilds take minutes, and how ordering a few lines makes them take seconds.
posts.content:
An image is a stack of read-only layers, one per build instruction. When a line changes, that layer and everything after it is rebuilt. That single fact explains almost every slow build.

Order from least to most volatile

Dependencies change rarely, source code changes constantly. Copy the dependency manifest first, download modules, and only then copy the rest of the tree.

FROM golang:1.27 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN go mod download          # cached until go.mod changes
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -o /out/app ./cmd/app

FROM gcr.example/distroless/static
COPY --from=build /out/app /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]

Before

Every commit invalidated the module download layer. Builds took about three minutes on CI.

After

Only the final two layers rebuild on a code change. Builds take about twenty seconds.

Multi-stage builds also keep compilers and caches out of the image you ship, which shrinks it and removes a whole class of security findings.

posts.title: CSS container queries: components that know their own size
posts.excerpt: Media queries ask about the viewport. Container queries ask about the space a component actually has.
posts.content:
A card in a wide main column and the same card in a narrow sidebar should not look identical. For years we faked this with modifier classes. Container queries make it a property of the component itself.

.card-list { container-type: inline-size; }

.card { display: grid; gap: 1rem; }

@container (min-width: 36rem) {
  .card { grid-template-columns: 12rem 1fr; }
}

Where they shine

  • Reusable cards, media objects and teasers
  • Dashboards with resizable panels
  • Design-system components that ship without layout assumptions

Pair them with clamp() and container units like cqi for type that scales with its box, not the window. Your components become portable in a way media queries never allowed.

Remember that an element cannot query itself: the container is always an ancestor.

comments.author: Lena
comments.content: The reminder about querying an ancestor got me twice last week.

posts.title: Table-driven tests that stay readable
posts.excerpt: Tables are great until they grow to forty columns. A few habits keep them easy to scan and to extend.
posts.content:
Table-driven tests are a Go tradition for good reason: adding a case is one line, and the loop body is written once. The trouble starts when the table becomes a spreadsheet nobody wants to read.

func TestSlugify(t *testing.T) {
    tests := map[string]struct {
        in, want string
    }{
        "spaces":     {"Hello World", "hello-world"},
        "symbols":    {"Go & Rust!", "go-rust"},
        "duplicates": {"a  --  b", "a-b"},
    }
    for name, tc := range tests {
        t.Run(name, func(t *testing.T) {
            if got := Slugify(tc.in); got != tc.want {
                t.Errorf("Slugify(%q) = %q, want %q", tc.in, got, tc.want)
            }
        })
    }
}

The version above is about as small as a table gets, and that is the point. Each row says what goes in and what should come out, and the subtest name tells you which row failed.

Habits that help

  • Name every case: a map key or a name field shows up in failure output.
  • Keep only the fields that vary; build the rest in the loop.
  • Split a table when cases need different assertions.
  • Print inputs and outputs in the error message, always.

A test you can read at a glance is a test people will keep up to date. That matters more than squeezing every scenario into a single table.

posts.title: Structured logs you will actually search
posts.excerpt: Logs are only useful if you can find the line you need at three in the morning. Structure is how.
posts.content:
Free-form log lines are written for the person who wrote them. Structured logs are written for the person who has to find them later, usually under pressure.

logger := slog.New(slog.NewJSONHandler(os.Stdout, nil))
logger.Info("payment captured",
    "order_id", order.ID,
    "amount_cents", order.Total,
    "duration_ms", time.Since(start).Milliseconds(),
)

A small field vocabulary

Agree on a handful of keys across services and stick to them. Consistency is what turns logs into something you can query.

  • request_id on every line of a request
  • user_id or account_id, never an email address
  • duration_ms as a number, not a string
  • error holding the error text only

If you cannot filter by it, it is decoration.

Start with the request ID. It is the single field that turns a pile of lines into a story you can follow.

comments.author: Tomás
comments.content: We banned string durations after a week of trying to sort them. Numbers or nothing.

posts.title: A pragmatic guide to rate limiting
posts.excerpt: Token buckets, sliding windows and what to send back when a client is over the limit.
posts.content:
Rate limits protect your service from bursts, buggy clients and the occasional bad actor. The algorithm matters less than choosing the right key and returning a response clients can act on.

Pick the key first

  • Per API key for authenticated traffic
  • Per IP address only as a coarse outer layer
  • Per route for expensive endpoints like search or exports

Token bucket in a few lines

limiter := rate.NewLimiter(rate.Limit(10), 20) // 10 per second, bursts of 20

func handler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    if !limiter.Allow() {
        w.Header().Set("Retry-After", "1")
        http.Error(w, "too many requests", http.StatusTooManyRequests)
        return
    }
    // ...
}

Always send 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header. Well-behaved clients will back off on their own, and the rest will show up clearly in your metrics.

In a fleet of servers, a per-process limiter allows N times the intended rate. Share state, or divide the limit by the number of instances.

posts.title: Five terminal habits that save me an hour a week
posts.excerpt: Small shell habits compound. These are the ones that stuck after years of trying new tricks.
posts.content:
None of these are clever. They are just the habits that survived, because each one removes a little friction many times a day.

  1. Reverse search everything. Ctrl + R beats retyping any command longer than ten characters.
  2. Name your aliases after verbs. serve, migrate, reset-db read like a to-do list.
  3. Keep a scratch directory. One throwaway folder per day for experiments.
  4. Make the prompt show the branch. Fewer commits on the wrong one.
  5. Learn one new flag a week. Most tools you use daily can do more than you think.
# ~/.config/shell/aliases
alias serve='go run ./cmd/app serve'
alias reset-db='dropdb app_dev && createdb app_dev && make migrate'
mkcd() { mkdir -p "$1" && cd "$1"; }

None of this needs a framework. A plain file of aliases and two small functions, kept in version control, travels with you to every new machine.

The best productivity tip is to notice when you type the same thing twice, and to automate it the third time.

comments.author: Sam
comments.content: The daily scratch directory is underrated. Mine is named after the date.
